Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Furthermore, a priori analysis confirms that the linearized EBU model accurately reconstructs reaction rate fluctuations from velocity fluctuations. Finally, an a posteriori application of the linearized models to LES spectra reveals significant agreement in both magnitude and frequency between the reacting flow's response to natural noise and its response to imposed acoustic noise. This success validates the linearized combustion model and the underlying assumption that reaction rate fluctuations caused by acoustic disturbances are simply a superposition of those generated by natural turbulence. As a result, this linearized model can predict flame response to acoustic disturbances and serves as a foundation for mode analysis to investigate thermoacoustic instabilities caused by such disturbances. The model file, along with directions for a priori and a posteriori analyses, is accessible at https://github.com/Mohamed-Ahmed-1997/Linearized_RANS. (See Also: Fluid Dynamics). The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. These findings indicate that the existence of a black hole LMXB population is consistent with neutron star LMXB observations, the millisecond pulsar population, and the activity levels of four known black hole candidates in the Galactic Centre. Finally, we propose specific criteria to distinguish between recurrent LMXBs that directly switch back to quiescence and those that form an accretion disk around a black hole before returning to quiescence.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Additionally, for the specific case where $k=2$, we prove that a planar embedding is possible if and only if the graph is a subgraph of a complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ with no induced four-cycle, a condition we can verify in linear time. Using a result from recent literature, we further establish that for $k\geq 3$, deciding if a planar drawing requires splitting exactly $k$ vertices is NP-complete. To conclude, we provide new results showing that finding minimum vertex split plans is optimal and scalable for real-world datasets, and we present a new hierarchy of plans that minimizes splits, edges, or vertices per pair of consecutive levels. Ultimately, we optimize this hierarchy to maximize the number of visible straight edges between any two levels. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, to mitigate this end-to-end threat, we proposed corresponding countermeasures. Our complete results are available at https://github.com/Aliakseiar/HyperDegrade-. Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. Furthermore, the algorithm scales effectively; for instance, computing the p-value for a dataset with one million data points required only 109 seconds. This exact algorithm enables researchers to explore non-parametric tests beyond the common mean comparison, opening up new research directions. Furthermore, the algorithm allows for the creation of rejection regions comprising all data permutations yielding a p-value of 0.01 or higher, offering a comprehensive view of the regions contributing to the final p-value. This study examines various mathematical models developed during the current pandemic to tackle key public health concerns regarding epidemic dynamics and their origins. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Furthermore, utilizing extended data ranges to parameterize models meant for short-term predictions can create misleading impressions of predictive power for future use cases. We conclude by addressing additional considerations for employing these models in real-time. Although differential equation models are not always the optimal choice for every epidemiological inquiry, alternatives such as compartmentless approaches should never replace them when the goal is to determine parameters for real-time implementation. Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Extensive comparisons among various iterative methods are conducted through extensive numerical experiments. These experiments also introduce a new metric, "accuracy-per-itertion+precomputation," to evaluate the efficiency of NS, NI, CN, and NN. The results indicate that NN generally surpasses NI and CI across most scenarios, with the optimal configuration being an NN3 method using an inception depth of one. Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical utility, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless applications where communication constraints often limit performance, particularly when contexts exist in a high-dimensional $d$-dimensional space. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, this work represents the first demonstration that high-dimensional contextual linear bandit regression can be solved without communicating the actual context vectors. To enable this, the agent-derived features are encoded into vectors of size $5d$, which are then decoded by the learner to construct the feature matrix used for optimization. Future research could explore scenarios where features are compressed to less than $5d$ per context or investigated when contexts follow a structured matrix format. Furthermore, if contexts are purely textual descriptions (e.g., product names), deriving the initial $5d$ feature vector could be achieved using deep neural networks, which would subsequently be decoded by the learner to optimize decisions.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10.
